lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Your AI second brain remembers everything.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Do you?

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: You ask your AI something hard,

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: and the answer is crystal clear.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: It all makes sense.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: You feel like you've learned it.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: But a week later, you ask the exact same question.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Memory fades fast at first, then slowly.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Researchers measured that curve in 1885,

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: and a 2015 replication found a similar curve.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: In a classic experiment, students studied short passages.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Then they re-read one passage.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: For another, they closed it and wrote down what they remembered.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Five minutes later, re-reading won, eighty-one percent to seventy-five.
lines.sub: Five minutes later, re-reading won: 81% to 75%.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: But after a week, it flipped.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Recalling beat re-reading, fifty-six percent to forty-two.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: In a second experiment, re-readers felt surest they'd remember,

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: yet remembered less.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: So after your AI explains something, close the answer,

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: say it from memory,

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: then come back at gaps that keep growing.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Spaced repetition tools like FSRS schedule those gaps for you.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Reading feels like learning.

lines.speaker: teacher
lines.text: Pulling it from memory, a little later each time, makes it stick.
